source_metadata.title: Impact of GLP-1 Analogue Therapy on Gastrointestinal Outcomes in Patients with Irritable Bowel Syndrome: A Real-World TriNetX Analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether initiating GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy after an IBS diagnosis was associated with subsequent coded gastrointestinal outcomes compared with no GLP-1 therapy.
This was a retrospective cohort study using de-identified electronic health records from the TriNetX Research Network.
The TriNetX Research Network dataset included 111 healthcare organizations across multiple countries, and the analyses were run on May 19, 2026.
Eligible patients were adults aged at least 18 years with IBS coded as ICD-10-CM K58; patients missing key demographic data were excluded.
Subtype analyses used IBS-D code K58.0 and IBS-C code K58.1.
The exposed cohort required a first prescription for semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, or tirzepatide within 30 or 90 days after the first IBS diagnosis.

exposures.details: First prescription of semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, or tirzepatide within the landmark window.

atoms.canonical_statement: The comparator cohort had IBS and no recorded use of any GLP-1 receptor agonist.

exposures.details: IBS diagnosis with no record of any GLP-1 receptor agonist use.

atoms.canonical_statement: The first IBS diagnosis was the index date; follow-up began at the 30- or 90-day landmark and continued for up to 5 years.

The study used separate 30- and 90-day landmark analyses to address immortal-time concerns; GLP-1 initiators had to start therapy within the relevant window and were described as event-free through the landmark for time-to-event analysis.

Propensity-score matching was 1:1 nearest-neighbor greedy matching with a 0.1 caliper using demographics, major disease-system comorbidities, and prior medication classes; standardized mean differences below 0.1 were considered acceptable.
Binary outcomes were summarized with risk ratios, odds ratios, and risk differences; time-to-first-event analyses used Kaplan-Meier curves, Cox-model hazard ratios, and log-rank tests.
The analysis also compared the number of coded outcome instances as a recurrence measure, with two-sided p<0.05 treated as statistically significant.
The study used only de-identified data and was reported as exempt from institutional review board approval.
Chronic diarrhea was defined from post-landmark ICD-10-CM coding (K52.9 or K59.1) and was treated as a healthcare-coded symptom event rather than necessarily a new clinical onset.

outcome.definition: First recorded post-landmark healthcare-coded symptom event (K52.9 or K59.1); interpreted as a subsequent coded event rather than necessarily true clinical incidence.

atoms.canonical_statement: After matching in the overall 30-day landmark analysis, 4,668 GLP-1 initiators were compared with 4,668 non-GLP-1 controls.
Table 1 showed post-match standardized differences below 0.1 across the displayed demographic, diagnosis, and medication variables.
After matching in the overall 90-day landmark analysis, 6,665 GLP-1 initiators were compared with 6,665 non-GLP-1 controls.
Table 2 showed post-match standardized differences below 0.1 across the displayed demographic, diagnosis, and medication variables.
After matching in the IBS-D 90-day analysis, 2,143 GLP-1 initiators were compared with 2,143 non-GLP-1 controls.
Table 3 showed post-match standardized differences below 0.1 across the displayed demographic, diagnosis, and medication variables.
After matching in the IBS-C 90-day analysis, 1,230 GLP-1 initiators were compared with 1,230 non-GLP-1 controls.

Table 4 showed post-match standardized differences below 0.1 across the displayed demographic, diagnosis, and medication variables, with the largest displayed imbalance still under the prespecified 0.1 threshold.
In the Overall IBS, 30-day landmark analysis, chronic diarrhea was recorded in 8.5% of GLP-1 users versus 9.5% of controls (risk ratio 0.894, 95% CI 0.786-1.017).

The authors concluded that GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation after IBS diagnosis was associated with lower subsequent coding rates for diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, and bloating/distension, including in IBS-D and IBS-C analyses, but emphasized that the findings are hypothesis-generating.
Causal effects cannot be inferred from the retrospective observational design, and residual confounding may remain despite propensity-score matching.
Important unmeasured factors included diet, baseline symptom severity, adherence, detailed IBS phenotype, health behaviors, and clinician follow-up patterns.
Reliance on ICD-10 diagnosis codes may undercapture or misclassify gastrointestinal symptoms.
Early discontinuation among patients who experience gastrointestinal intolerance could select for GLP-1 users who tolerate therapy better, creating survivor bias.
Time-to-first-event analyses may reflect healthcare utilization and coding recurrence rather than true symptom onset or total relapsing-remitting IBS burden.
The design required IBS diagnosis before GLP-1 initiation, so the results may not generalize to patients who develop IBS-like symptoms after starting GLP-1 therapy.
Potential indirect effects of weight loss, glycemic improvement, or reduced systemic inflammation could contribute to observed IBS outcome differences.

The source contains an interpretive ambiguity between the landmark description of remaining event-free to the landmark and a later statement that patients with pre-landmark outcomes were included in the primary analysis.

The reported median times to first abdominal-pain coding in the 30-day analysis (1,985 and 1,857 days) exceed a strict five-year horizon, creating a numerical inconsistency with the stated follow-up of up to 5 years.
The authors reported no financial or non-financial competing interests related to the work.
The article states that no datasets were generated or analyzed during the current study.
